title: Talk in more ways
why: Every new chat is the same kind: it comes from one ghostly1 invite, starts on the DHT when no direct path exists and goes live by itself. Next is what a chat shows about the other person, and more clients.
gate: Every client tested against every other one, on each transport it offers.

now.text: One ghostly1 invite code, a QR and a ghostly.tools link
Chats with pinned keys, files of any size, payments and local apps
A chat with no direct path starts on the DHT and goes live by itself; short texts over the DHT when the live link drops
Calls and screen sharing in every chat, while it is live; Linux desktops call with their own media
Pairing progress you can watch while two apps find each other
Voice messages, rich text, mentions, link previews and cards for invites, payments and identities
Replies, edits, emoji reactions, delivery marks, videos that play in the chat, and pictures or files pasted or dropped into a chat
A typing indicator in one-to-one chats, which you can turn off
A headless CLI for bots that joins the same chats, calls included

next.text: Presence, a capability of its own that you can keep private
Native apps for iOS and Android (route to be decided)

title: More ways to pay
why: One payment agreement, many wallets. Each method keeps its own rules and its own risks.
gate: Disposable-network settlement, fee limits, unknown-result reconciliation, and recovery or exit tested before any mainnet claim.

now.text: Mainnet and Testnet wallets side by side, a confirmation before real money moves
Cashu and Lightning, through the mint or your own sources (NWC, LND, Core Lightning, WebLN, Breez, Fedimint), several Lightning cards per network
Lightning addresses, and paying a request from any wallet
Ark (Arkade and Bark), Spark, Fedimint, USDT and on-chain bitcoin, experimental; BDK on test networks only
Spark, Breez and Fedimint on Mainnet (Spark and Breez with your own Breez API key; Fedimint not yet tried with real funds)

next.text: Mainnet for the BDK on-chain wallet, once reviewed with real money in mind
Unilateral exit for Ark
Liquid and other rails

title: Reach each other in more places
why: New transports widen where two people can meet. Each one is an adapter both sides must support, never a silent bridge.
gate: Each adapter tested on its own platforms, with its relays and privacy trade-offs stated.

now.text: WebRTC (not on Linux desktops); Iroh and HyperDHT between desktop apps
Iroh in the browser through n0's relays; HyperDHT there only through a relay you set

next.text: Local network discovery, generic QUIC and WebSocket relay profiles
Tor, libp2p, Pear / Holepunch components

title: Keep things, bring them back
why: Profiles, backups and held messages exist. Next is making recovery routine.
gate: Restore drills across devices and versions, without overwriting anything.

now.text: Local profiles, sealed backups to a file or S3, messages held for an away contact

next.text: Scheduled backups and retention
More storage places (WebDAV, Blossom and others), for backups and held messages

title: Bring an identity, only if you want
why: Nobody needs a public identity to talk. Proofs are optional, several can coexist, and you choose what each contact sees.
gate: Sessions without any proof still work. Proving a key never implies importing a graph or permission to publish.

now.text: Proofs made once, shared per chat: Nostr, Pubky (approved in Pubky Ring or Passport), a domain, an OpenPGP or SSH key, a Bitcoin address, a DID
Nostr social layer: profile, follows and notes; posting off by default
A did:dht for every profile, listing only the identities you switch on
Public profiles on identity cards, and a contact shown as one of their identities

next.text: Bluesky / AT Protocol accounts: built, blocked until the website's OAuth client document is live on ghostly.tools
OpenID accounts (Google, Microsoft, Apple, GitLab, Twitch): built, blocked until Ghostly's OAuth clients are registered
Hardware wallets as signers, and passkeys
Keet, blocked until it offers a supported signing API
Pubky profiles and content

title: From a conversation to a community
why: Groups need membership, roles and distribution designed together, off the DHT.
gate: Membership authority, removal, partitions, abuse limits and recovery tested.

now.text: Private groups of up to eight and communities of up to 256: text, a picture and payments between members

next.text: Files and calls in groups, each a capability of its own
More than one admin, member key updates
Channels, topics and gated access
Group encryption beyond the epoch-key scheme (MLS)

title: SDKs, adapters and plugins
why: Let others build pieces without forking the app. A plugin is packaging; the contract stays a WISP.
gate: Malicious-plugin tests, provenance and an update policy.

now.text: Contracts as WISP drafts, @ghostly/sdk in the repository (an adapter registers as a plugin), and a headless CLI with an event stream for bots

next.text: Adapter manifests, and the SDK and the CLI published on npm
Package authenticity and updates
A permissioned plugin host

title: Apps and catalogs
why: Mini-apps, peer-to-peer games, commerce, interfaces for specific contracts, all found through independent catalogs.

next.text: Mini-apps and games
Independent catalogs, several indexers, perhaps an indexer contract
Reputation and optional paid apps

title: A Ghostly you can host
why: An always-on runtime (even a Raspberry Pi at home) so services and presence don't depend on an open tab.
gate: Measured hardware needs, secure administration, backup, reboot and upgrade tests.

next.text: Self-hosted 24h runtime
Ghostly OS
